response: {"text":"The phenomenon of moving the subject pronoun to the front of a question that starts with a wh‑word, for example “what you have?” instead of the usual “what have you?”, has been noted in informal speech. Earlier investigators reported it among speakers of a Caribbean variety and suggested it might reflect English influence. Later observations found the same pattern in a neighboring variety, while it was absent among speakers from a different region, indicating that simple borrowing does not explain it. This note does not offer a solution but highlights linguistic quirks that deserve further study. Because the construction occurs only in casual conversation, systematic data are scarce and sometimes contradictory. The informal second‑person singular pronoun, and occasionally formal plural forms, are the most common subjects in this structure, although speakers say other pronouns and even proper names can appear, with some names sounding odd. Some informants feel the fronted form is the natural everyday version, whereas the inverted version sounds marked or confrontational.
